title: Diff Gate
user: 3–30 person software teams using coding agents who need a responsible engineer to understand, constrain, and approve an agent-produced change before merge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A small team using Cursor asks what code review becomes when LLMs generate more of the code.
A 256-reaction Claude Code request asks for a VS Code diff-review UI comparable to Copilot Edits Review.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 developer communities identify review friction as agent-assisted output rises; it is release-blocking rather than a convenience pain.
current_workaround: Open huge PR diffs, rely on agent prose summaries, or ask a second agent to review the first.
incumbents_and_gap: GitHub, GitLab, Copilot Edits, and Cursor expose diffs, but none makes repo-specific policy, evidence, risky-file escalation, and an accountable approval packet the default unit for small teams.
smallest_useful_product: GitHub app that turns one agent PR into a policy-tagged review packet: changed contracts, migrations, tests run, risky paths, and required owner sign-off. Non-goals: generating code, replacing Git hosting, or autonomous merges.
success_measure: In five pilot teams, 80% of agent-authored PRs have an identified owner and test evidence before merge, while median review time does not rise by more than 15%.
monetization: subscription — $12/developer/month or $99/team/month is justified by recurring protected merge workflow and audit history.
constraints: Least-privilege GitHub permissions; never train on repository code; configurable retention; keep security findings advisory until independently verified.
why_distinct: It is a review-control surface for accountable change, not another coding agent or generic PR summarizer.

title: Team Skills Registry
user: Engineering leads standardizing several coding agents who need reusable, reviewable instructions and safe rollout across repositories.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A team asks how others are changing their SDLC and identifying bottlenecks in an AI-heavy workflow.
A 454-reaction request asks for AGENTS.md and .agents/skills support, noting the community has asked since August 2025.

recurrence: The request accumulated 454 reactions and the SDLC question is independent evidence that teams are operationalizing agents rather than experimenting alone.
current_workaround: Copy AGENTS.md files between repos, paste prompts into a wiki, or let each developer maintain private instructions.
incumbents_and_gap: GitHub repos, Notion, and vendor-specific project memory store text, but do not provide a signed, versioned compatibility layer for one skill across agent vendors and repositories.
smallest_useful_product: Hosted registry with Git-backed skill packages, target-agent adapters, approval/ring rollout, and an execution receipt naming the exact skill version. Non-goals: model hosting, prompt marketplace, or automated code execution.
success_measure: Three pilot teams publish 20+ shared skills and can attribute 90% of governed agent runs to a reviewed version within 60 days.
monetization: subscription — $149/team/month for governed private registries and audit history; the value rises with every repository and agent vendor.
constraints: Treat instructions as untrusted code; support secret references rather than secret text; preserve repository access boundaries and vendor licenses.
why_distinct: The wedge is controlled distribution and provenance of team behavior, not a thin prompt library.

title: Client Context Firewall
user: Freelance developers juggling client engagements with AI tools who need to preserve their own voice while preventing context, accounts, and deliverables from bleeding between clients.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A freelancer says AI-assisted speed has reset market expectations and asks how to retain professional identity.
A 505-reaction feature request asks for multiple accounts for the same connector in Claude and Claude Code.

recurrence: A freelancer-facing identity concern and a 505-reaction multi-account request point to the same recurring multi-context workflow problem.
current_workaround: Separate browser profiles, manually swap API keys, keep notes in disconnected folders, and hope the active chat has the right client context.
incumbents_and_gap: 1Password, browser profiles, and vendor workspaces separate logins but do not bind a client brief, allowed sources, style guide, connectors, and final delivery trail into an agent session boundary.
smallest_useful_product: Desktop companion that launches named client workspaces with scoped connectors, encrypted local context bundles, redaction rules, and a deliverable provenance export. Non-goals: employee surveillance, hosted source-code storage, or a new IDE.
success_measure: Ten freelancers complete 30 client sessions with zero cross-client connector use and report a 25% reduction in setup time.
monetization: subscription — $19/month is plausible for contractors whose client isolation and setup time recur every workday.
constraints: Client data must remain device-local by default; clear keychain integration; no claims of absolute data-loss prevention; support export/deletion for offboarding.
why_distinct: It protects the working boundary of a client engagement rather than being a generic AI chat organizer.

title: Agent Capacity Ledger
user: Small engineering teams paying for several AI coding subscriptions and APIs who need to plan capacity, understand limits, and hand work over before a paid seat is unexpectedly exhausted.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An operator asks how teams actually operate an expanding OSS AI infrastructure stack.
A 724-reaction report says a paid Max subscription hits usage limits instantly.

recurrence: The 724-reaction paid-limit report and separate operations discussion show capacity uncertainty is both common and operationally costly.
current_workaround: Read opaque vendor dashboards, screenshot quota messages in Slack, or maintain a spreadsheet of subscriptions and fallback accounts.
incumbents_and_gap: Vendor dashboards cover one product and FinOps tools target cloud invoices; neither models human-agent work queues, vendor limits, and permitted fallback paths across coding tools.
smallest_useful_product: Team ledger that ingests usage exports or local opt-in events, forecasts remaining useful sessions, assigns approved fallback tools, and records cost per project. Non-goals: model proxying, credential sharing, or bypassing vendor limits.
success_measure: Pilot teams attribute 90% of paid agent spend to a project and cut work interruptions caused by unexpected limits by 50% in one billing cycle.
monetization: subscription — $79/team/month tracks recurring spend, policy, and capacity decisions.
constraints: Never collect prompts by default; respect each vendor's terms and account-sharing rules; estimates must be labeled as estimates.
why_distinct: It manages work capacity under real vendor constraints, not merely token metering or an LLM router.

title: Project Memory Release
user: Product engineers whose agent must use project decisions, architecture, and product language correctly as a codebase changes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Developers discuss tools getting worse through complexity, feature growth, and enterprise defaults, and ask what people switched to.
A 613-reaction request asks to connect Claude Code to Claude Projects knowledge bases.

recurrence: The 613 reactions show project context is a broad unmet expectation, while the HN thread warns against another opaque, overbuilt workspace.
current_workaround: Paste README excerpts into chats, maintain stale wiki pages, or hope an agent's proprietary project memory has the current decisions.
incumbents_and_gap: Notion, GitHub wikis, and vendor project-memory features store information, but lack a release workflow that turns approved decision changes into small, testable context packs across tools.
smallest_useful_product: A Git-native service that compiles selected ADRs, glossary terms, and product decisions into versioned context packs, highlights stale citations, and emits vendor-neutral references. Non-goals: vector database hosting, chat UI, or automatic documentation writing.
success_measure: In pilots, 75% of agent PRs cite a current context-pack version and stale decision references fall by 40% over two releases.
monetization: subscription — $99/team/month for recurring context releases, access control, and provenance.
constraints: Do not index repositories by default; use scoped Git access; preserve document permissions; make generated packs reviewable before release.
why_distinct: The product is a release process for trusted project knowledge, not generic RAG over company files.

title: Portable Agent Workspaces
user: Independent developers and small teams moving between terminals, cloud VMs, and coding agents who need settings, guardrails, and local state to travel predictably without hand-maintained dotfile surgery.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A developer reports that GitHub notification email is full after replying to an issue notification, illustrating fragile tool-state dependencies.
A 444-reaction issue says Claude Code does not respect the XDG Base Directory specification.

recurrence: The 444 reactions indicate strong demand for predictable local-tool behavior; operational breakage appears when small defaults leak across environments.
current_workaround: Use dotfile repos, shell aliases, copied config folders, and undocumented cleanup scripts.
incumbents_and_gap: chezmoi, Nix, and dev containers are powerful but are not agent-aware: they do not distinguish portable policies from machine-local sessions, credentials, and caches.
smallest_useful_product: CLI plus signed manifest that packages approved agent settings, skills, sandbox rules, and path mappings; it validates XDG/container placement and produces a reversible install receipt. Non-goals: a package manager, secret vault, or remote desktop.
success_measure: A pilot can move a governed workspace to a fresh macOS/Linux machine in under 15 minutes with no policy-path violations.
monetization: subscription — $10/developer/month for private workspace registries, fleet policy, and support; local core remains usable free.
constraints: Never copy credentials by default; require explicit path allowlists; preserve OS package licenses; provide full uninstall and dry-run modes.
why_distinct: It adds agent-specific portability and separation of policy versus ephemeral state, not another dotfile manager.

title: LSP Readiness Check
user: Small product teams onboarding contributors to agent-assisted repositories who need language intelligence, code navigation, and validation working before an agent is allowed to change code.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A prospective OSS maintainer asks how to systematically discover real industry gaps rather than build speculative projects.
A 566-reaction Codex request asks for automatic detection and installation of Language Server Protocol support.

recurrence: A 566-reaction request identifies setup friction at the exact dependency agents need to reason safely about unfamiliar codebases.
current_workaround: Read setup docs, install language servers one by one, or accept degraded agent edits in repositories with partial tooling.
incumbents_and_gap: Dev containers and IDE extensions install environments, but do not supply a repo-specific proof that an agent has navigation, diagnostics, formatting, and test commands available and healthy.
smallest_useful_product: GitHub app/CLI that runs a disposable readiness probe, inventories available LSP capabilities and commands, and emits an agent-readable signed capability file. Non-goals: hosting language servers, an IDE, or autonomous dependency upgrades.
success_measure: 80% of onboarding PRs in pilot repos pass the readiness contract before agent changes start, and environment-related review failures drop by 30%.
monetization: subscription — $49/repository/month for private CI checks, policy templates, and readiness history.
constraints: Run probes in isolated containers; do not transmit source code; pin installers and verify provenance; respect repository build costs.
why_distinct: It verifies usable semantic tooling as a release gate rather than simply auto-installing extensions.

title: Change Recovery Ledger
user: Developers supervising agents across long sessions who need to safely inspect, revert, and selectively replay changes after an agent takes a wrong turn.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Developers report dramatically more and larger PRs and ask how others approach code review.
A 461-reaction Codex request asks to bring back /undo after unintended changes.

recurrence: The 461-reaction undo request and increased PR volume indicate that recoverability is a daily control need, not a rare editor preference.
current_workaround: Use Git reflog, stash patches, manually reset files, or abandon an entire agent session when one change is suspect.
incumbents_and_gap: Git retains commits and IDE undo retains local edits, but neither captures the semantic intent, command trail, generated files, and safe partial reversal of a multi-step agent operation.
smallest_useful_product: Local agent sidecar that checkpoints file groups and commands, shows intent-linked change sets, and supports tested selective reversal/replay as a patch. Non-goals: cloud code backup, Git replacement, or running the agent itself.
success_measure: Pilot developers recover a mistaken agent change in under five minutes in 80% of seeded scenarios without discarding unrelated work.
monetization: subscription — $15/developer/month for persistent history, team policy, and encrypted recovery export.
constraints: Local encryption and configurable retention; patches may contain secrets; never auto-run a replay; integrate with Git without altering history silently.
why_distinct: It is semantic, partial recovery for agent operations, not a prettier Git UI or a one-button undo.

title: Spoken Dev Brief
user: Small distributed product teams who think through implementation aloud and need fleeting spoken decisions to become attributable, code-linked engineering briefs without handing meeting recordings to another silo.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A macOS user asks for a meeting-transcription daemon after losing the ability to export notes from Granola into Obsidian.
A 265-reaction request asks for push-to-talk voice transcription in the Codex IDE extension.

recurrence: The two requests independently want voice capture to stay portable and near development work rather than trapped in a meeting product.
current_workaround: Record in a meeting app, copy an AI summary into a ticket, or leave voice notes unsearchable and detached from the code decision.
incumbents_and_gap: Granola, Otter, and Fireflies transcribe meetings; issue trackers store decisions. The gap is a private, developer-oriented decision brief that links claims to repository paths and requires human confirmation.
smallest_useful_product: Local-first recorder that transcribes selected speech, proposes a short decision/assumption/open-question brief with repository references, and exports to Markdown/Jira after approval. Non-goals: meeting bot, HR analytics, or autonomous code generation.
success_measure: At least 60% of pilot recordings produce an approved engineering brief, and approved briefs are opened from a PR or issue within seven days.
monetization: subscription — $12/user/month covers recurring private transcription, local model updates, and integrations.
constraints: Explicit consent indicator; local transcription option; retention controls; no covert recording; speech and code must not be used to train models.
why_distinct: The deliverable is a confirmed engineering decision record, not a generic transcript or AI meeting summary.

title: BYOK Code Policy
user: Small agencies and regulated product teams allowing developers to bring approved AI model keys who need enforceable data, cost, and model rules without buying one vendor's entire coding suite.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A team asks where manual QA fits while AI accelerates autocomplete, coding, review, and automated testing.
A 253-reaction request asks VS Code to support BYOK/custom models for inline code completions.

recurrence: BYOK demand is explicit and highly reacted-to; QA leaders need proof that accelerated development stayed within the team's safety boundary.
current_workaround: Publish a policy PDF, trust developers to select the right endpoint, or prohibit useful tools entirely.
incumbents_and_gap: Vendor enterprise plans impose one ecosystem; API gateways route traffic. Neither provides lightweight, developer-visible preflight policy plus verifiable evidence tied to a code change.
smallest_useful_product: Local/CI policy client that checks repo classification, approved model/region/key source, cost ceiling, and required QA evidence, then writes a signed compliance receipt to the PR. Non-goals: a model proxy, secret reseller, or surveillance dashboard.
success_measure: In pilots, 95% of AI-assisted PRs have a policy receipt and no restricted repository is sent to an unapproved endpoint over 60 days.
monetization: subscription — $15/developer/month for policy packs, audit retention, and administrator controls.
constraints: Avoid collecting prompts/code; integrate with secrets managers; legal claims must be reviewed by customers; endpoint classifications need transparent overrides.
why_distinct: It supplies evidence-backed policy at the change boundary, not a thin wrapper that forwards LLM calls.

title: Agent Protocol Console
user: Indie software teams adopting MCP/ACP-connected tools who need to see which agent capability changed, what it can now access, and whether a downstream workflow needs attention.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A developer asks whether anyone is using MCP server-to-client notifications for list changes, progress, and logs, noting little practical discussion.
A 348-reaction request asks VS Code to support Agent Client Protocol for third-party agent integration.

recurrence: The protocol request has 348 reactions and the HN thread shows practical notification semantics are still unsettled as integrations proliferate.
current_workaround: Read extension changelogs, inspect logs after something breaks, or let every tool send its own opaque notifications.
incumbents_and_gap: Datadog and generic webhook tools observe infrastructure, while agent vendors expose their own logs. The gap is a capability-focused console for tool permissions, schema changes, and human routing across protocols.
smallest_useful_product: Self-hostable gateway/console that records declared MCP/ACP capabilities and selected lifecycle events, diffs permission/schema changes, and sends one actionable owner notification. Non-goals: running arbitrary remote tools, prompt logging, or a generic automation platform.
success_measure: Pilot teams identify 90% of configured agent-tool capability changes within one hour and keep false-positive owner alerts below one per tool per week.
monetization: freemium — free self-hosted single workspace; $99/team/month for managed retention, access controls, and multi-workspace routing.
constraints: Store metadata rather than prompts/tool payloads by default; verify protocol authentication; isolate untrusted tool descriptions; respect provider terms.
why_distinct: It governs changing agent capabilities, rather than proxying generic webhooks or adding another agent chat surface.

title: Agent Task Packets
user: Small software teams evaluating products or accepting client work who need a repeatable, vendor-neutral way to give an agent representative data, acceptance tests, constraints, and a safe demo environment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An accounting client evaluating POS systems is unhappy with a prior purchase and asks whether mockup data can be requested from SaaS salespeople.
A 263-reaction proposal asks for a standard folder where agent skills should live across agent harnesses.

recurrence: The evaluator needs realistic proof before a costly commitment; the 263-reaction standardization request shows pressure to make agent work portable rather than vendor-bound.
current_workaround: Use a sales demo, share sensitive customer exports, assemble an ad-hoc spreadsheet, or write one-off setup instructions for every evaluation.
incumbents_and_gap: Demo environments, Postman collections, and synthetic-data vendors cover fragments. None treats an evaluation as a portable, auditable packet combining de-identified data, scenario assertions, skill instructions, and a teardown clock.
smallest_useful_product: Web service and CLI that packages schema-preserving synthetic fixtures, acceptance scenarios, allowed skills, and reset scripts into expiring signed task packets. Non-goals: generating production customer data, full test-management replacement, or autonomous procurement decisions.
success_measure: Five pilot evaluators execute 10+ representative scenarios before purchase and detect at least one workflow mismatch that a vendor demo missed.
monetization: subscription — $149/workspace/month for reusable private packets, evaluator seats, and audit exports; high-stakes evaluations recur across clients and vendors.
constraints: Strong de-identification and synthetic-data disclosure; do not circumvent SaaS trial limits; customer must own data rights; packets need expiry and deletion controls.
why_distinct: It makes pre-purchase proof reproducible and safe, rather than being a generic mock-data generator or prompt pack.
